To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a binding-site model for inactivation that depends only on calcium entry predicts well the results of single- and double-pulse experiments on Ca channels in cardiac muscle cells.
the model of inactivation presented here can explain the experimental results and that the model is a binding-site model for inactivation that depends upon Ca entry.

a binding-site model for Ca channel inactivation can explain many experimental results, that this model can account for the nonexponential turn-off of Ca channels, and that the model suggests that the two-pulse experiments of Tsien and colleagues are not consistent with a voltage-dependent component for Ca channel inactivity or with two populations of Ca channel.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms by which Ca channel activity is regulated.
the mechanism of calcium channel inactivation.
the mechanism by which calcium entry causes inactivation of calcium channels.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our model is a plausible explanation of the experimental results.
a binding-site model of inactivation can explain all available data.
the binding-site model for inactivation is consistent with the available data and is the simplest mechanism consistent with these data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
inactivation depends on Ca entry and that Ca channels inactivate in an all-or-none manner.
the Ca current inactivation mechanism is a binding-site model, and that Ca entry is the cause of the binding.
Ca entry through the membrane is sufficient to account for the observed properties of Ca channel inactivation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca channel inactivation is a dynamic process that depends on Ca influx, and the rate of inactivation depends on Ca influx.
Ca channel inactivation can be modeled as a binding-site mechanism in which Ca entry is necessary for inactivation, but not sufficient to explain the kinetics of inactivation.
Ca channel inactivation is not simply the result of Ca binding to a site at or near the internal mouth of the channel.
